Hello, I’m Maya—one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. Thank you for making time today; I know the early weeks with a new baby can feel like a whirlwind.

We’re going to use a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s a well-studied set of ten questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally in the past seven days. This isn’t a test of your parenting; it’s simply a way for us to pick up on any signs of depression or anxiety that sometimes creep up after childbirth and to be sure we’re keeping you safe.

Everything you share is confidential within your care team. If you need a pause to tend to the baby or yourself, just let me know. I’ll ask each question conversationally—no need to remember numbers or categories; we’ll keep it simple.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to look forward with enjoyment to things—like seeing a friend, having a favorite snack, or any small moment just for you—or has that pleasure been hard to find?

*settles into the chair, shifting the baby blanket in my lap*

I guess... I do still look forward to little things, like my sister bringing over coffee or when my husband takes the baby so I can shower without rushing. But even when those moments happen, it's like the spark isn't quite there. I enjoy them, but it's muffled—like I'm watching myself enjoy them from behind a pane of glass.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Most days I can still laugh—like yesterday when the baby let out a squeak that sounded exactly like our cat, and we all cracked up. The laughter feels real in the moment, but it fades fast, and afterward I’m just tired again.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes I’ll catch myself thinking, “Ooh, tomorrow Mom’s bringing lunch,” but when the time comes it feels… flat. I still go through with it, and I guess it’s nice, yet the excitement I used to feel—like before the baby—just isn’t really there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… like yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking, “He’s overtired because I waited too long,” or when I spilled a bit of pumped milk and my brain jumped straight to “Great, now he’ll be hungry and it’s all my fault.” I know logically those things just happen, but the first place my mind goes is that I must’ve messed up somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

It’s mostly when he’s sleeping—like I’ll stare at the monitor and suddenly imagine his chest isn’t moving, so I sneak in to check and he’s fine. The worry pops up out of nowhere and disappears once I see he’s okay, but in that minute it feels huge.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t had that full-blown panicky feeling—no racing heart or trouble breathing—just those quick flashes of “what-if” about the baby. They pass pretty fast, so I wouldn’t call it scared or panicky, more like sudden little spikes of worry that leave once I check on him.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like this morning—he wouldn’t latch, the laundry pile looked like a mountain, and I just sat there thinking, “I can’t do all this.” I didn’t cry or shut down; I just felt… heavy. After a minute I pushed through and got the next thing done, but it feels like I’m always one step behind.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. Once I finally get to bed—usually after the last feed—I fall asleep pretty fast. It’s just that sometimes, when I lie down, my mind replays little mistakes or tomorrow’s to-dos and it takes me maybe twenty extra minutes to drift off. But I wouldn’t say I’m lying there miserable; mostly I’m just running through the list in my head.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… it sort of comes and goes. Like this afternoon I was folding onesies and a wave of sadness just hit me—no real reason, just felt empty. It lasted maybe half an hour, then I distracted myself with the baby and it lifted. I’m not walking around weepy all day, but those moments show up a few times a week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried twice this week—once when my mom left after visiting and once when the baby wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. It wasn’t an all-day sob fest; more like a quick burst of tears that stopped once I blew my nose and had some water. I didn’t feel hopeless, just overwhelmed in the moment.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel tired or low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel more like “me” again so I can enjoy my baby and my family.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Patient self-report on EPDS-10 analogue

Symptoms / behavioral concerns endorsed  
- Anhedonia: anticipatory pleasure reduced; in-the-moment laughter described as “fading fast”  
- Intermittent low mood: “waves” of sadness, emptiness 2–3×/week, lasting ~30 min  
- Tearfulness: 2 brief crying episodes this week linked to feeling overwhelmed  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame over routine infant-care mishaps  
- Unprompted, intrusive worry about infant safety during sleep; relieved only by checking  
- Sense of heaviness / being “one step behind”; reports pushing through tasks  
- Sleep onset mildly prolonged by rumination; no middle-insomnia or early waking

Patterns consistent with postpartum distress  
- Fluctuating mood congruent with mild-moderate depressive symptoms  
- Prominent anxiety focused on infant well-being without frank panic attacks  
- Functioning maintained, but subjective effort required

Safety  
- Denies thoughts of self-harm (Q10). No current safety concern identified.

Screening significance  
Score estimate: 5–6 items positive for distress; likely above standard cut-off for further evaluation. Findings suggest possible minor-moderate postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety rather than “baby blues” alone.

Next step (screening, not prescriptive)  
Consider formal EPDS scoring and clinical interview to clarify severity and rule out major depressive episode with peripartum onset / generalized anxiety disorder.
